newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori tells Peru rebels no one backs them.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori tells Peru rebels no one backs them.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori left Lima on Tuesday for the first time since Peru's four-week hostage crisis began, visiting the site of one of his main victories against leftist rebels.
He used the trip to proclaim that no one in the country supported the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holding 74 hostages at the Japanese mabassador's home in Lima.
Government negotiator Domingo Palermo said he was still waiting for the MRTA reply to his proposal that a "guarantor commission" be set up to oversee a peaceful end to the 28-day-old crisis.

Fujimori took Ecuador's President Abdala Bucaram, who is in Peru on an official visit, to the Andean mountain province of Ayacucho and showed him the village of Vilcashuaman, a former centre of guerrilla activity that has been placed back under government control.

"All Peruvians have clearly demonstrated that the people reject violence," Fujimori told a cheering crowd against the dramatic Andean backdrop. "All of Peru is against this hostage-taking and demands their freedom."
Maoist Shining Path guerrillas began their revolution in Ayacucho and controlled large areas throughout the 1980s, but were ousted by government forces in the early 1990s.
Fujimori says he has broken the back of Shining Path and the previously less-known Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movemement (MRTA), and that the MRTA are acting out of desperation.

Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a close friend of the president named by the Vatican to sit on the proposed guarantor commission, travelled with Fujimori and called on all sides to sit down for talks as soon as possible.

"My constant request is that God move everyone as soon as possible to start a dialogue which surely will bring peace," Cipriani said. "Please, trusting in God, trusting in truth and openness, sit down to talk. We wish for this, and I believe it will soon happen."

Red Cross spokeswoman Cecilia Baux told Reuters the organisation would join the commission if and when it is formally set up. "We can participate in the commission but only in matters of a humanitarian nature," she said.
The government and MRTA would fill the final two places on the commission proposed by Palermo.
At the residence on Tuesday was a quiet day after two shooting incidents there in the previous 24 hours.
The shootings caused no injuries and two hostages who appeared briefly at a window late in the afternoon indicated that everyone inside was well.
The two Asian-looking men gave energetic thumbs-up signals to shouted questions from nearby journalists as to their health and how they were being treated.
The approximately 15 rebels, who stormed a reception at the residence on Dec. 17, originally took hundreds of guests hostage.

They have released the majority in what they called "goodwill gestures," hanging onto dozens of top Peruvian government and security force officials, the younger brother of Fujimori, and Japanese diplomats and businessmen, as bargaining chips to secure their main demand that hundreds of jailed comrades be freed.
Fujimori has flatly refused to meet this demand but has said he will not use force to end the siege unless the hostages are harmed.
His firm position received praise from Bucaram.
"The world supports Peru and its president not backing down in its position because it would set a very bad precedent to negotiate with people who employ chaos and violence," he said.
The rebels are armed with rifles and grenades and have booby-trapped and mined the compound against surprise attack.
A police source told Reuters on Tuesday the 15 rebels were hand- picked and trained at a remote jungle hideout by two former guerrillas from El Salvador for a month before the attack.
